header.incumbent: Homegrown billing system, built by an engineer who has since left
header.tag_why: The CFO froze all new vendor projects, but this deal was already exposed: Owen said he couldn't get it past Diane 'without a number that's ours', we sent the generic ROI deck instead, and finance still saw the project as 'a nice to have' when the freeze hit.

evidence.excerpt: There wasn't one big thing.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: The billing system is homegrown, built by a guy who left, and every pricing change takes them a quarter.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: He wanted it done before they launched a new pricing tier, but the tier didn't have a date either.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: There was no compelling event. The pain belonged to one person: Owen's long-held wish, with no deadline and an undated pricing tier. The real urgency was latent and nobody surfaced it: key-person risk on a system whose builder left, and a quarter lost on every pricing change. That is why it lost to 'if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded'.
trigger.messaging: Lead homegrown-billing prospects with the cost of standing still, framed as key-person risk plus a quarter of roadmap per pricing change, so the champion has an urgency story that finance can fund.

evidence.excerpt: The CFO, I guess? Diane.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Owen told me. I never spoke to her.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: No. Owen said he'd bring her in at the end.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: "I can't get this past Diane without a number that's ours."
evidence.label: quote

decider.insight: Diane held the budget gate, and the champion said so explicitly. Yet the plan was to 'bring her in at the end', and the rep never spoke to her. Everything we know about her, including that the freeze was blanket and not aimed at us, comes only through Owen. Owen's own words show the deal needed her before any freeze happened.
decider.messaging: Give champions a CFO-ready artifact and position an early finance conversation as part of our process, not an end-stage formality, because product-only messaging never reaches the person who funds it.

evidence.excerpt: There wasn't one. It was us against doing nothing.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Owen never looked at anybody else, as far as I know.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Toward the end Owen started asking for things for finance.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: "do you have something that shows payback?"
evidence.label: quote

competitor.insight: The competitor was the status quo plus the CFO's budget priorities, and absence of other vendors is only 'as far as I know'. The meaningful change in questions was the shift to finance about a month before the freeze. That was the economic buyer surfacing through the champion, and we answered it with generic material.
competitor.messaging: Against do-nothing, our message has to price the status quo, so we need a cost-of-inaction story in the customer's own numbers, not a feature comparison.

evidence.excerpt: "that's a quarter of roadmap in five minutes."
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: "we're not trying to grow revenue with billing, we're trying to stop it being a tax on the roadmap."
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: We only ever talked to product and engineering.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: The demo landed in roadmap-speed terms: price changes, trials and proration in minutes instead of a quarter. Our M7 revenue framing didn't get silence; Owen actively rejected it. The rep first claimed nothing fell flat. Every message was aimed at product and engineering, so finance never received any message at all.
message.messaging: For homegrown-billing replacements, swap M7's 'grow revenue' for an engineering-capacity claim: pricing changes in minutes, not a quarter of roadmap.

evidence.excerpt: I sent him the ROI deck. The general one, with the study.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We were going to set up a session to build one. Then Q3 closed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Before that we were in procurement. Well, we'd sent paper.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They missed their number in Q3 and she put a hold on all new vendor projects.
evidence.label: fact

decided.insight: The rep felt it slip only at the freeze email, but the decisive window was the month before. Owen asked for payback, got the generic M6 study deck, said it wouldn't work, and the session to build a real number never happened. 'In procurement' was really 'sent paper'. 'It's timing' hides that finance had already classed this as a nice-to-have that a freeze would cut first.
decided.messaging: Replace M6's 'independent economic impact study' with an offer to build the customer's own payback number, because a third-party study failed with exactly the buyer it was meant for.

evidence.excerpt: The number. Their own. What the homegrown system costs them.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: he mentioned once that some landlord subscriptions lapse because the card fails and nobody chases it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We never added it up.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: We had a doc for that. He wanted to talk to someone who'd done it.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: The main gap was not missing product. We had the ingredients for their number: engineering time, billing errors, and lapsed landlord subscriptions from failed cards (exactly what M10 recovery addresses). We just never added them up. Migration was a second gap: no card re-collection, a staged move, and a 'don't touch billing before renewal season' blackout. A doc existed, but Owen wanted a peer reference and the transcript doesn't show he got one.
gaps.messaging: Package a cost-of-homegrown-billing model (engineering hours, billing errors, recovered failed-card revenue) plus a migration reference customer who moved subscriptions without re-collecting cards.

evidence.excerpt: a tax on the roadmap
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: "if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded."
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Owen said finance saw it as a nice to have.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: "I can't get this past Diane without a number that's ours."
evidence.label: quote

language.insight: The customer talked in terms of cost and burden: 'tax on the roadmap', 'a number that's ours'. We talked about growth and generic proof: 'grow revenue', 'the study'. Finance's words ('on fire', 'nice to have') show what was missing: evidence that the status quo was burning money.
language.messaging: Adopt 'billing shouldn't be a tax on your roadmap' as the hook for homegrown-billing prospects, paired with 'your number, not our study' for finance.

gaps.question: Was the freeze truly blanket, and did Diane ever see what the homegrown system costs?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen: was any vendor project exempted from the freeze, and has Diane seen a cost figure for the current billing system?

gaps.question: Will the deal really come back next year, and when is renewal season?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen: what would have to be true for finance to fund this next year, and when is the renewal-season blackout for billing changes?

gaps.question: Did Owen evaluate any other vendor or a rebuild in-house?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen directly whether anyone else was considered, including rebuilding in-house.

gaps.question: Which parts of the pitch got silence?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee: besides revenue framing, which slides or claims (e.g., ROI study, support, reconciliation) drew no follow-up from Owen or his engineers?

gaps.question: Was a migration reference customer ever offered or arranged?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee: did Owen speak to a customer who migrated subscriptions without re-collecting cards, and if not, why not?

gaps.question: How big are the failed-card lapses and billing errors?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen (or his engineering lead) for rough monthly lapsed-subscription counts and engineering hours spent on billing, to seed the payback model now.

close.rep_takeaway: When a champion asks 'do you have something that shows payback?', that's the economic buyer talking through them. Treat it as the most urgent item in the deal: build their own number that week from what they've already told you (here: engineering time, billing errors, failed-card lapses), and ask to present it to the CFO yourself. A freeze is easiest to survive when finance already knows what the status quo costs, so 'nothing we could have done' is worth re-examining here, since there was a month to act.
